data.howToName: How to boil hard-boiled eggs at altitude

description: At 5,000 ft water boils at 94.9°C, so a large fridge egg needs 12 minutes 20 seconds to hard-boil. Times by size and altitude, from the Williams formula.

examples.result: One large fridge egg, hard-boiled at 3,000 ft: 11 minutes 20 seconds.
steps: The egg starts at fridge temperature, 4°C, and the water boils at 96.9°C at 3,000 feet.
The hard target is 84°C at the edge of the yolk.
The formula gives 681 seconds, about 11 minutes 20 seconds.
examples.title: One large fridge egg, hard-boiled at 3,000 ft

examples.result: One extra-large fridge egg, hard-boiled at 5,000 ft: 13 minutes 20 seconds.
steps: The egg starts at fridge temperature, 4°C, and the water boils at 94.9°C at 5,000 feet.
The formula gives 799 seconds, about 13 minutes 20 seconds.
examples.title: One extra-large fridge egg, hard-boiled at 5,000 ft

faqs.answer: Because the boiling point falls as air pressure falls, about 1°C for every 300 meters of altitude. Water boils at 100°C at sea level, 96.9°C at 3,000 feet, 94.9°C at 5,000 feet, and 92.9°C at 7,000 feet. Cooler water cooks the egg more slowly.
faqs.question: Why does altitude change the boiling time?

faqs.answer: Yes. A large fridge egg needs 13 minutes 30 seconds to hard-boil at 7,000 feet. The hard target of 84°C still sits below the 92.9°C boil there. It is only at much greater heights, where water boils below the target, that a hard-boiled egg becomes impossible.
faqs.question: Can I hard-boil an egg at 7,000 feet?

faqs.answer: It keeps the water level up, but it does not change the boiling point. Air pressure sets the boiling point, not the lid. Use a lid at altitude because the water evaporates faster, and keep the pot generous so the level stays above the eggs.
faqs.question: Does a lid help at altitude?

faqs.answer: Williams himself warned the formula under-predicts at altitude. On Mount Washington in 1917, an egg that needed 3 minutes lower down took 5 minutes at 1,917 meters, more than the formula predicted. Coagulation slows as the temperature falls. Treat the calculator's high-altitude times as a floor and check one egg before cooling the batch.
faqs.question: Why did my mountain eggs come out underdone?

faqs.answer: Less than hard eggs, because the 63°C soft target sits further from the boiling point. A large fridge egg needs 5 minutes 10 seconds to soft-boil at 5,000 feet, against 4 minutes 30 seconds at sea level. The hard time grows by more than two minutes over the same climb.
faqs.question: How much longer do soft eggs take at altitude?

felicityNote: If you cook at altitude, the timer on the box is wrong for you. The boiling point is the number that matters, and the calculator has it.

parts.meaning: The constant from the egg's thermal properties: density 1.038 g per cubic cm, specific heat 3.7, thermal conductivity 0.0054.
The weight of the egg in grams. A large egg is 57 g (USDA size).
The starting temperature of the egg: 4°C from the fridge, 20°C at room temperature.
The boiling point of the water: 94.9°C at 5,000 feet, against 100°C at sea level.
The target temperature at the edge of the yolk: 84°C for hard-boiled.
The yolk edge factor. The yolk is about a third of the egg, so its edge sits about 69 percent of the way from the center to the shell.

formula.text: Time = 27 × M^(2/3) × ln(0.76 × (Tegg - Twater) / (Tyolk - Twater)). For a large fridge egg at 5,000 feet, hard-boiled: 27 × 57^(2/3) × ln(0.76 × (4 - 94.9) / (84 - 94.9)) = 740 seconds, about 12 minutes 20 seconds.

howToSteps.name: Know your altitude
howToSteps.text: Water boils at 96.9°C at 3,000 feet, 94.9°C at 5,000 feet, and 92.9°C at 7,000 feet. Pick the closest setting on the calculator.

howToSteps.name: Boil a generous pot
howToSteps.text: Use plenty of water and a lid. Water evaporates faster up high, and the level must stay above the eggs for the whole cook.

howToSteps.name: Lower the eggs in
howToSteps.text: Lower each egg in gently on a spoon and start the timer at once. Keep the water at a steady boil.

howToSteps.name: Time it
howToSteps.text: At 5,000 feet, boil a large fridge egg for 12 minutes 20 seconds. A medium egg needs 11 minutes 20 seconds, an extra-large 13 minutes 20 seconds, and a jumbo 14 minutes 15 seconds.

howToSteps.name: Check one, then cool
howToSteps.text: Lift one egg out, cool it under cold water, and cut it open. If the yolk is not set, give the rest one more minute, then move them all to ice water.

lede: At 5,000 feet water boils at 94.9°C instead of 100°C, so a large fridge egg needs 12 minutes 20 seconds to hard-boil instead of 10 minutes 10 seconds. The cooler the water, the longer the heat takes to reach the yolk.

title: How Long to Boil Eggs at Altitude
tutorial: Water boils cooler the higher you go, because the air presses down less hard on the pot. At 3,000 feet it boils at 96.9°C, at 5,000 feet at 94.9°C, and at 7,000 feet at 92.9°C. The egg still needs its yolk edge to reach 84°C for hard-boiled, but the heat has less push behind it, so everything takes longer.

For a large fridge egg the hard-boiled time grows from 10 minutes 10 seconds at sea level to 11 minutes 20 seconds at 3,000 feet, 12 minutes 20 seconds at 5,000 feet, and 13 minutes 30 seconds at 7,000 feet. Soft eggs stretch less in absolute terms, from 4 minutes 30 seconds to 5 minutes 25 seconds at 7,000 feet, because their 63°C target sits further from the boiling point.

The hard target is the one that suffers most at altitude, because 84°C sits close to a 92.9°C boil at 7,000 feet. The last few degrees take the longest, and that is why the hard time grows by more than three minutes while the soft time grows by less than one. If you live high up, hard-boiled eggs are where the calculator earns its keep.

Williams himself warned that the formula under-predicts at altitude. On Mount Washington in 1917, an egg that needed 3 minutes lower down took 5 minutes at 1,917 meters, more than the formula predicted. Coagulation is a chemical process that slows as the temperature falls, not a switch that flips at one temperature. Treat the calculator's high-altitude times as a floor: check one egg before you cool the batch, and add a minute if the yolk is not set.

One practical note: at altitude the water also evaporates faster, so use a lid and a generous pot of water. The lid does not change the boiling point, air pressure sets that, but it keeps the water level up and the boil steady while the eggs cook.
